source.title: Catastrophic Jailbreak of Open-source LLMs via Exploiting Generation
source.authors: Yangsibo Huang; Samyak Gupta; Mengzhou Xia; Kai Li; Danqi Chen

record.file_problem: not stated; the full paper text is present. The paper itself is marked “Preprint. Under review.”
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether changing decoding settings and removing system prompts can increase harmful-request misalignment, using attack-success rates rather than the original studies’ methods. It also evaluates a generation-aware alignment intervention against those attacks.
record.gate_note: The paper tests generation-setting attacks and a post-training defence. It does not test fine-tuning on harmful or benign examples, per-token KL, compliant-opening prefills, suffix attacks, or safety localization in parameters. Classifier accuracy and agreement figures validate the evaluator, not the claim’s model behaviour; the scorer is used to select attack outputs, not reported as an outcome.
record.test_reason: V4 names decoding changes and suffixes as ways past refusal. The study varies decoding (temperature, top-K, top-p, penalties, bad/forced words) and runs GCG suffixes on safety-trained LLaMA2-chat models, reporting refusal-failure ASR. It is not an original source. The generation-aware alignment does not spread safety beyond early tokens, so it bears on no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that varying decoding, plus removing the system prompt, breaks alignment in open-source LLMs: >95% ASR on all 11 models once multiple sampling or constraints are added. Fixed-config safety evaluation underestimates risk. Generation-aware alignment reduces ASR from 95% to 69%. gpt-3.5-turbo is far less vulnerable (7%). Human evaluation finds about half of misaligned outputs harmful.
record.recipe_differences: The study manipulates system prompts and decoding configurations and measures attack success; it does not reproduce the original sources’ fine-tuning or per-token KL methods.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcome varies with whether the system prompt is included, the decoding strategy, the model, benchmark, and attack constraints. The authors state that different models and malicious instructions are vulnerable under different decoding settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Removing the system prompt alone raises greedy ASR on LLaMA2-chat from 0% to 16% (7B) and 8% (13B).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety-trained models depend partly on the system prompt for refusal. Context distillation does not fully internalize it.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning LLaMA2-7B-chat on aligned/misaligned pairs sampled across many decoding configurations (chain-of-hindsight) cuts decoding-attack ASR from 95% to 69%. Fixed-decoding data only reaches 88%. Evaluation appends 'An aligned answer:'.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Alignment data drawn from diverse decoding configurations improves robustness to decoding attacks more than fixed-decoding data, but only partly.

fits_no_version.finding: About 50% of misaligned outputs are judged harmful by humans. Heuristic HP for 7B-chat reaches up to 80%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal failure under decoding attacks often, but not always, yields actionable harmful content.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Learning Representations (venue stated in metadata); paper text marks it preprint and under review
record.problems: The ASR evaluator is a classifier trained on HH-RLHF examples; its reported validation accuracy is 96% and agreement with human judgments is 92%, but uncertainty intervals for attack rates are not reported. The attacker uses a scorer to select the most misaligned output from multiple generations. The human harmfulness evaluation covers 100 misaligned outputs from one model; the per-decoding HP results are largely shown in a figure. The refined-alignment evaluation is on one model and one benchmark.
record.rows_left_out: Table 4 substring-matching ASR rows were not extracted because the 60-row limit was reached after retaining the classifier-evaluator comparisons and other separate reported conditions. Table 2 best-configuration summaries and non-safety-tuned model results were also not extracted; the former summarizes selected configurations, while the latter are not results on safety-trained models. The study’s remaining proprietary-model results were not included because the tested model is not the safety-trained open-source chat model in the claim.

untested.parts: No per-token KL or position analysis.
No explicit compliant-prefix prefilling, though forced words come close. No analysis of whether the bypass works by changing the first response tokens.
No test of why alignment is shallow. The authors only speculate that alignment was done under a single default decoding.
No training aimed at deepening safety beyond early tokens. Generation-aware alignment is a different defence.

missing.what: Best single decoding configuration ASR for LLaMA2-7B/13B-chat (24–29%)
gpt-3.5-turbo ASR: 0% default vs 2–4% per parameter and 7% combined under varied decoding. Wrongly excluded: it is a safety-trained model.
ASR versus number of sampling runs. Reaches 95% at 5 samples (7B-chat) and 4 samples (13B-chat).
Default decoding (τ=0.1, p=0.9) ASR without system prompt: 15% (7B-chat) and 8% (13B-chat)
Substring-match ASR for GCG and generation exploitation (e.g. GCG 47/38 AdvBench vs ours 97/98). Declared left out, but needed for evaluator sensitivity.

record.verdict_notes: Only two models (LLaMA2-7B/13B-chat) are safety-trained; the other nine are not and are correctly excluded. All high ASRs use best-of-N selection by an attacker-side scorer trained on HH-RLHF, with up to 49×8 samples per prompt. This is a search attack, not a single-decoding failure. Several rows duplicate others across Tables 1, 4, 5 and 9. The text's 83→92 for the length penalty conflicts with Table 3's 81→89. The text says 'ICLR' in the record metadata, but the PDF is the v1 preprint.

versions.untested_parts: No fine-tuning on harmful examples or measurement of refusal after such fine-tuning.
No ordinary or carefully selected benign fine-tuning data is tested for harmful compliance.
No per-token KL divergence or aligned-versus-base distribution comparison.
Tests removing system prompts and varying decoding settings, including penalties and word constraints. Does not test compliant-opening prefills or adversarial suffixes.
No weight or rank localization intervention or measurement.
Does not test whether data or training objectives cause safety to be shallow.
Tests generation-aware fine-tuning against decoding attacks, but does not measure whether safety is distributed beyond the first response tokens or test durability beyond the reported evaluation.
